about.title: Sergi Cebrián
about.subtitle: From stumbling into archery by accident at Vall de Núria to the Spanish National Team and building an independent school in Terrassa.
about.bioLead: My name is Sergi Cebrián, and I've been immersed in sports since I was very young. I've practiced many—martial arts, swimming, football—but most seriously snowboarding, hockey (which I still play today), and archery.
bioParagraphsBeforeCallout: I discovered archery in 2010 purely by accident while trying different outdoor activities at Vall de Núria, and it hooked me from the very first moment—from the very first arrow. I have to admit shooting came quite naturally to me, and very early on I started standing out among those around me.

My competitive streak and the athletic upbringing shaped by practicing so many sports led me to debut in official tournaments—and even at a Spanish National Championship—less than six months after shooting my first arrow. Looking back with perspective, I can say those results were genuinely strong. Yet one thing that surprised me right away was how casual and recreational the sport still felt, even inside a National Championship. It became clear to me that both the sport itself and I had a long road ahead.

I started out shooting Barebow, completely self-taught, studying how Olympic archers shot on television. I quickly spotted the gap between the more 'instinctive' styles and the procedures executed by professional archers. My first goal was to develop my own homegrown technique that would allow me to shoot any type of bow the exact same way. That defined the first half of my career: I soon began winning medals across Catalonia and Spain, and my competitive and training experience never stopped growing.
about.epiphanyIntro: Everything I learned through tournaments, travel, and the thousands of arrows I shot every month led me to a realization that changed my life:
about.epiphanyCallout: The secret wasn't in a spotless textbook technique, a specific school, or any rigid line of work—the secret of archery lies in your head, your heart, and the emotions with which you live what you do. And when it comes to those three things, there are no secrets.
bioParagraphsAfterCallout: I've been fortunate to travel widely and live in places like the United States and Sweden, dedicating 100% of my time there to shooting more arrows, soaking up how archery is lived abroad, and stepping into Olympic Recurve. I walked away from a discipline where I was stacking up Catalan, Spanish, and international medals just to start over again as a beginner. In this new chapter, though, I had the privilege of working under the wing of former Spanish National Coach and current USA Archery Head Coach Elías Cuesta—truly one of the greats. Unlike the rest of my career, I finally had a coach, and that gave me priceless growth in every sense.

Those were 10 months of relentless work and fresh knowledge, exploring techniques very different from what I was used to. I was living in Sweden at the time, and COVID and distance eventually parted our ways, leaving me with lasting lessons on how things must be done—and just as importantly, what things need to be stripped away.

With the recurve bow I have never shown the effortless touch I had with barebow, yet through sheer work I built a strong medal record in Catalonia and Spain, earning international selection with the Spanish National Team in Field Archery.

My independence and conviction in my own way of working led me to create 'La Cova del Drac'—an archery school and technical training center where I put my passion and experience at the disposal of anyone who wants to share this wonderful sport with me.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.subtitle: Archery is undoubtedly a technical sport, yet by no means complicated: technique must adapt to our body, never the other way around.
methodology.introText: There is the basic 'ballistic' aspect, followed by a clear set of technical principles that need to be met—but under no circumstances do I believe that technique or any specific school, whether KSL, Continuous Shot, or any other, should force an archer into shooting one rigid, prescribed way.

rules.title: COMFORT
rules.subtitle: Technique adapts to our body
rules.description: Through my own experience and that of fellow archers over the years, one thing has become crystal clear: technique is what must adapt to our body, rather than subordinating the archer to a rigid school.

rules.title: SYSTEM
rules.subtitle: From routine to the pleasure of shooting
rules.description: Training methodology is what ultimately separates monotonous routine from genuine pleasure on the line—and our results depend on it. Some drills assimilate concepts, others raise performance, and others build workload capacity; every training goal must match the work performed.

rules.title: BALANCE
rules.subtitle: Translating concepts into sensations
rules.description: Across more than ten years coaching archers, I've realized the hardest thing for everyone is truly grasping the basic concept of the shot—and harder still, translating that concept into physical sensations. That is my core pillar for guiding any archer to an advanced level. It looks simple, yet it isn't.

psychology.bridgeText: Building on these three points as our working pillars, we can tackle the fundamental side of this sport—where I pour all my effort and where my athletes stand out above the rest:
psychology.title: Psychology & the Emotional Side
psychology.description: I studied ethology and apply my knowledge of behavioral science to prepare my athletes emotionally—because that is what truly makes the difference.

pillars.title: Stepping out of the comfort zone
pillars.description: Once technical comfort is built, I pull my athletes out of that comfort zone so they learn to respond under real challenge.

pillars.title: True competitive mindset
pillars.description: I prepare them psychologically for the demands of sport and head-to-head competition.

pillars.title: Managing frustration
pillars.description: I teach them how to handle frustration so a rough arrow becomes fuel for growth rather than baggage on the next shot.

pillars.title: Optimal emotional flow
pillars.description: Most importantly, I give them practical tools to generate and sustain an optimal emotional flow for every moment.

psychology.quote: I don't consider myself a great archer, yet I have always had the ability to perform above my level when it mattered—and that can be passed on too.

facilities.title: Facilities
facilities.subtitle: Purpose-built spaces on Carrer Major de Sant Pere in Terrassa covering every need of an athlete—from amateur to professional.
facilities.introLead: My desire to share my knowledge and experience as an athlete goes far beyond handing out a few outdated little lessons.
introParagraphs: When I started shooting a bow, my workouts boiled down to flinging arrows indiscriminately—pretty much like everyone else does at first—until I quickly saw that lacking a system and methodology never brings growth proportional to the work put in.

Archery is a sport like any other: real progress demands a clear working system and physical conditioning tailored to the activity. Dedicating myself exclusively to archery allowed me not only to gain the knowledge needed to compete internationally, but also to create the ideal spaces to cover every need of an athlete, from amateur to professional.

Anyone who starts a sporting project with me gets not only my knowledge, but my entire infrastructure to facilitate and maximize their growth. Time has taught me that leading by example and doing joint field work alongside my athletes is the best way to walk with them as far as they want to go.
